## A model bake-off with partial dependence plots

::: {.lab-meta}
[Week 6]{} [Reading: Valavi et al. (2022)]{} [GLM · CART · RF · BRT · Maxent]{}
:::

A virtual species responds linearly to elevation and has a hump-shaped (quadratic) response to annual precipitation. Seven models are fit to the same presence/absence data: correctly specified and misspecified GLMs, a classification tree, a random forest, boosted regression trees, and Maxent. The random forest, boosted trees, and Maxent are tuned on a validation set, then all models are compared on a separate test set with ROC curves. Two-variable partial dependence plots show what each model actually learned about elevation and precipitation, which we can check against the true surface.

* A partial dependence plot averages a model's predictions over the observed values of the other variables. That shows the learned relationship for any model, including ones without coefficients.
* A correctly specified model recovers the true shape best. Flexible machine-learning models approximate it, with more noise. A misspecified GLM can miss it entirely.
* Tune on validation data and judge on separate test data. Small AUC differences between tuning settings are often noise, and it's worth checking argument names: a misspelled `regmult` is silently ignored.

## Marginal vs. partial effects

::: {.lab-meta}
[Weeks 4–6]{} [Interpreting fitted models]{} [GLM · RF · BRT]{}
:::

A virtual species with a quadratic term and an interaction is used to compare two ways of showing one variable's effect. A **marginal** effect holds the other variables at their means. A **partial** effect averages predictions over the observed values of the other variables. Both are computed for the true probability function and for a boosted regression tree, a random forest, and a misspecified GLM, and overlaid. A two-variable partial surface then shows how well the boosted trees recover the true interaction.

* Marginal and partial effects differ whenever the model is nonlinear (even just through the logistic link) or has interactions. Correlated predictors make the choice matter more.
* Comparing against the known truth separates errors in the model from differences caused by which summary you chose.
* Effect curves are least reliable where data are sparse. Check the rug of observed values before interpreting the tails.

## Information leakage

::: {.lab-meta}
[Week 2]{} [Reading: Roberts et al. (2017)]{} [Evaluation · transferability]{}
:::

A species responds only to precipitation seasonality, but the model is given a *proxy* instead. The proxy tracks seasonality closely south of 45°N and is pure noise north of it. A logistic regression on the proxy, trained and tested on a random split of southern data, looks good (AUC around 0.85). Applied to new northern data, it is no better than a coin flip. The southern test residuals are strongly spatially autocorrelated (a Moran's I test), the warning sign that random holdouts let information leak between training and test data.

* A random train/test split of spatially clustered data can overstate how well a model will transfer to new places.
* A proxy correlated with the true driver predicts well wherever the correlation holds, and fails completely where it doesn't.
* Spatial autocorrelation in residuals is a diagnostic that an evaluation may be too optimistic. Whether blocked cross-validation would catch a contrived case like this one is left as an open question.

## Point process models

::: {.lab-meta}
[Week 6]{} [Readings: Renner et al. (2015) and its Appendix S1; Valavi et al. (2022)]{} [IPPs · DWPR · background points · BRT · Maxent · sampling bias]{}
:::

This demo turns an abundance surface λ into the intensity of an *inhomogeneous Poisson process* (IPP), draws random point patterns from it, and then fits a point process model back to one pattern, treated as presence-only records. Following the supplementary material of Renner et al. (2015), the model is fitted with *downweighted Poisson regression* (an ordinary weighted Poisson GLM) and, in R, also with spatstat's `ppm()`. The estimates are compared with the known true coefficients. The demo then asks how many background (quadrature) points are enough. It refits with increasing numbers of random points to see when the log-likelihood settles down, the same check as Figure 1 of Valavi et al. (2022). It then compares that with the standard-error formula |A|·s/√n, which gives the number of points needed for a chosen accuracy. Next, the same weights turn flexible methods into point process models: a Poisson boosted regression tree (gbm in R, scikit-learn in Python) and Maxent (maxnet or elapid). On a second species with a hump-shaped response, a threshold, and a linear effect, both are compared with a linear GLM on independent test data and by their response curves. Finally, the records of the first species are re-simulated with survey effort concentrated around towns. A PPM that ignores the bias is checked with Ripley's K function, and three remedies are compared: a bias covariate, an area-interaction model of the extra clustering, and spatial thinning of the records (spThin).

* An IPP's intensity λ(s) is the expected number of points per unit area. Its log-likelihood includes the integral of λ, and background points are a device for estimating that integral, not absences.
* Downweighted Poisson regression fits an IPP with any GLM software. Unlike presence–background logistic regression (and Maxent's raw output), it estimates the intensity on its true scale.
* Any method that fits a weighted Poisson regression can fit a point process model with the same DWPR weights, including boosted regression trees. When responses are strongly nonlinear, these flexible point process models (and Maxent) far outperform a linear GLM.
* The integral's standard error, |A|·s/√n, says how many background points a model needs. For this species it's more than 40,000 for a 2-unit tolerance, well above Maxent's default of 10,000.
* Sampling bias that is correlated with the environment biases the slopes, not just the intercept, and the model's standard errors don't warn you. The inhomogeneous K function detects the leftover clustering. A measured bias covariate fixes it best; an area-interaction model and spatial thinning help only partly, and thinning has costs of its own.
